The explicit frozen-contact example has the stated occupancy and embedding.Two scope points should be explicit in the final note:Under an arbitrary feasible exterior, the exact bundle count, maximum increase, and uniqueness assertions concern bundles supported on  $C$ , or their restrictions to  $C$ . They count all global bundles in the displayed baseline configuration because that configuration has no other matching edges.The supplied excerpt does not define tile charge. The universal freezing argument is validThe key distinction is between remaining occupied and remaining an endpoint. Your proof uses the former correctly.Let  $\mathcal B$  be the set of feasible bundles for the original configuration, allowing the empty move for convenience. For  $v\in P$ , write  $m(v)$  for its original matching mate.The exact retention principle is
$$v\text{ cannot be promoted by any }B\in\mathcal B
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m(v)\text{ remains occupied under every }B\in\mathcal B.
\tag{9}$$
Indeed, the only way a bundle can make  $m(v)$  blank is to select their matching edge and promote  $v$ .Thus a frozen vertex universally retains its mate, although that mate may subsequently be labeled  $T$  rather than  $P$ . Also, a vertex with two distinct universally retained occupied neighbors cannot be promoted.These principles quantify over arbitrary feasible bundles. They are not statements merely about a particular order of attempted moves or a particular finite search.The four inductions are acyclicYour certificate can be written in the following order.StageVertices frozenTwo occupied neighbors certifying each step1Top even vertices from column  $0$  through  $a$ At column  $0$ : the north and west  $T$ . Thereafter: the north  $T$  and preceding odd top vertex, retained as the mate of the preceding frozen even vertex.2Bottom even vertices from column  $W-1$  backwards through  $a$ At column  $W-1$ : the south and east  $T$ . Thereafter: the south  $T$  and following odd bottom vertex, retained by the preceding freezing step.3Bottom odd vertices on the left, moving outward from  $a-1$ The vertical top neighbor, retained by Stage 1, and the right bottom neighbor, retained either centrally or by the preceding step of Stage 3.4Top odd vertices on the right, moving outward from  $a+1$ The vertical bottom neighbor, retained by Stage 2, and the left top neighbor, retained either centrally or by the preceding step of Stage 4.In Stages 1 and 2, the last vertices frozen are the two central endpoints. By (9), both central endpoints are therefore universally occupied, and their matching edge cannot be selected.Every premise used in Stages 3 and 4 has already been established. Each obstruction uses two distinct neighbors. There is no circular argument involving the central edge or the outward inductions.The resulting frozen set contains exactly the claimed candidates:
$$\begin{aligned}
&\{(r,c):c<a,\ r+c\equiv0\pmod2\},\\
&\{(r,c):c>a,\ r+c\equiv1\pmod2\},\\
&\{(0,a),(1,a)\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}$$
Attainment makes the frozen set exactThe displayed set  $U$  contains one endpoint of every noncentral matching edge and no endpoint of the central edge.Its feasibility argument is correct:Within each half,  $U$  is one checkerboard color.The central column separates the halves, so no promoted vertex in one half is adjacent to a promoted vertex in the other.At an even column, a promoted vertex has its perpendicular  $T$ -support and no occupied neighbor inside  $C$ .At an odd column, a promoted vertex has no perpendicular support and can have only the adjacent central endpoint as an occupied neighbor.The two axial  $T$ -supports touch the frozen corner endpoints, not  $U$ .Original  $T$ -vertices only lose occupied neighbors.Therefore every vertex of  $U$  occurs in a feasible bundle and is not frozen. Combined with (10), this proves
$$\boxed{\text{The universally frozen set is exactly }C\setminus U.}
\tag{11}$$
This certifies more than a sufficient freezing procedure: it identifies the entire universal frozen set.2. The prefix implications are necessary and sufficientThis is the most important part of the classification to check independently. Direct occupied-degree formulas give precisely your system.Treat  $x_i,y_i$  as Boolean variables and set
$$x_k=0.
\tag{12}$$
The sentinel represents the fact that the next top even endpoint at the end of the left half is the central endpoint, which remains occupied.By the freezing theorem, the listed  $x_i,y_i$  orientations are the only possible left-half promotions.Exact condition for  $y_i$ Suppose  $y_i=1$ , so  $(1,2i)$  is promoted.Its matching mate is deleted. Its other possible occupied neighbors are:its south  $T$ , always occupied;its upper neighbor, deleted exactly when  $x_i=1$ ;for  $i>0$ , its left neighbor, deleted exactly when  $y_{i-1}=1$ .For  $i=0$ , the left lateral site is blank. Consequently its occupied degree is exactly
$$1+(1-x_i)+\mathbf1_{\{i>0\}}(1-y_{i-1}).
\tag{13}$$
Requiring this to be at most one gives exactly
$$y_i\Rightarrow x_i,
\qquad
y_i\Rightarrow y_{i-1}\quad(i>0).
\tag{14}$$
Exact condition for  $x_i$ Suppose  $x_i=1$ , so  $(0,2i+1)$  is promoted.Its matching mate is deleted, and its north site is blank. The remaining possible occupied neighbors are:the lower odd endpoint, deleted exactly when  $y_i=1$ ;the next upper even endpoint, deleted exactly when  $x_{i+1}=1$ , with convention (12).Its occupied degree is therefore exactly
$$(1-y_i)+(1-x_{i+1}).
\tag{15}$$
Requiring this to be at most one is equivalent to
$$x_i\Rightarrow(y_i\lor x_{i+1}).
\tag{16}$$
Equations (13) and (15) account for every neighbor of every promoted left vertex. Original  $T$ -vertices remain feasible by monotonicity of the occupied set, and retained  $P$ -vertices have no imposed degree bound. Therefore (14)–(16) are sufficient as well as necessary.In particular, the proof does not silently require the intermediate or final pair to satisfy an additional terminality condition.The common-prefix conclusion follows exactlyYour terminating-successor argument works. A shorter equivalent proof makes the conclusion especially transparent.Let
$$X=\{i:x_i=1\},
\qquad
Y=\{i:y_i=1\}.$$
If  $X=\varnothing$ , then  $Y=\varnothing$  by  $y_i\Rightarrow x_i$ .Otherwise let  $h=\max X$ . We have  $x_{h+1}=0$ , either by maximality or by (12). Hence (16) forces  $y_h=1$ . The backward implications in (14) then force
$$y_0=\cdots=y_h=1,$$
and  $y_i\Rightarrow x_i$  forces
$$x_0=\cdots=x_h=1.$$
No  $y_i$  with  $i>h$  can occur, since it would force  $x_i=1$ .Thus
$$X=Y=\{0,\ldots,h\}.
\tag{17}$$
Conversely, every such common prefix, including the empty prefix, satisfies the system.There are therefore exactly  $k+1$  feasible left restrictions, each deleting both horizontal matching edges in its first  $i$  blocks.3. The right suffix, product count, and square count are correctThe right-half argument is the reflected version of the left-half argument. For complete precision when  $k\ne l$ , one can use
$$(r,c)\longmapsto(1-r,W-1-c).
\tag{18}$$
This takes the instance with parameters  $(k,l)$  to the instance with parameters  $(l,k)$ , interchanging the two ends and the candidate colors.The phrase “reflection across the central column and interchange of the rows” is understandable as a local reflected argument. It should not be read as claiming that the entire same instance has that symmetry when the two half-lengths differ. Formula (18) avoids that minor ambiguity.Applying the left result with the exchanged parameters gives exactly  $l+1$  right restrictions: the last  $j$  complete right blocks, where  $0\le j\le l$ .The two choices are independentThe central column remains occupied in every feasible bundle. No promoted vertex in the left half has a neighbor in the right half, and neither half can change a central endpoint’s status.Therefore the left and right feasibility conditions are independent. Every pair
$$(i,j)\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\times\{0,\ldots,l\}
\tag{19}$$
gives a feasible local bundle.Conversely, every feasible local bundle has exactly one such pair of restrictions. There is no additional orientation multiplicity: the freezing theorem has already fixed the only allowable orientation of each selected noncentral edge.Thus (19) is a bijection, and only  $(0,0)$  is empty. This proves
$$\boxed{\#\{\text{nonempty feasible bundles supported on }C\}
=(k+1)(l+1)-1.}
\tag{20}$$
The product-of-chains assertion follows under inclusion of oriented matching-edge sets.Exact remaining endpoint setFor the bundle  $(i,j)$ , the remaining endpoints are precisely
$$P'\cap C
=
\{0,1\}\times
\{2i,2i+1,\ldots,W-1-2j\}.
\tag{21}$$
This is a full two-row rectangle of width
$$W-2(i+j)
=
2(k-i)+2(l-j)+1.$$
It consequently has exactly
$$\boxed{2(k-i)+2(l-j)}
\tag{22}$$
all- $P$  unit squares.The bundle selects exactly
$$2(i+j)$$
matching edges. Formula (22) vanishes if and only if
$$i=k,\qquad j=l,$$
because both  $k-i$  and  $l-j$  are nonnegative.Therefore  $U=(k,l)$  is indeed:the unique greatest feasible local bundle under inclusion;the unique local bundle of maximum size  $W-1$ ;the unique local bundle removing every endpoint square.The mixed-color necessity assertion also follows. A color- $0$  bundle has no left promotion and retains all  $2k$  left-and-center squares. A color- $1$  bundle retains all  $2l$  right-and-center squares. Since  $k,l\ge1$ , both colors are necessary for square elimination.4. The arbitrary-exterior extension is valid, with local numerical scopeThere is a useful justification that I recommend adding explicitly: the prescribed supports force every other contact site of  $C$  to be blank.An additional occupied neighbor of  $C$  cannot be  $P$ , because  $C$  must remain a complete endpoint component.The only unprescribed perpendicular contact sites occur at odd columns. Each is adjacent to a prescribed even-column  $T$ -support. That support already has its occupied endpoint neighbor in  $C$ , so the odd-column contact site must be blank.Likewise, the two unused axial contact sites,
$$(1,-1),\qquad (0,W),$$
are adjacent to the prescribed axial  $T$ -supports
$$(0,-1),\qquad (1,W),$$
respectively. Those supports already have their occupied neighbors in  $C$ , so the unused axial sites must also be blank.Hence every feasible exterior retaining  $C$  and the listed supports gives each endpoint of  $C$  exactly the same occupied exterior neighbors as in the baseline construction. Freezing, attainment, and classification all survive unchanged.What remains localIn the explicitly padded baseline,
$$|T|=2(k+l+1)+2=W+3,
\qquad
|M|=W,$$
so the stated objective  $2W+3$  is correct. The baseline is also single-terminal.With arbitrary additional exterior components: $W+3$  counts the prescribed supports, not necessarily all global  $T$ . $W-1$  is the maximum promotion increase contributed by  $C$ .Formula (20) counts nonempty bundles supported on  $C$ . $U$  is the unique largest and square-removing local bundle.The endpoints in  $C$  remain single-terminal initially; additional components need not be.For example, let  $N(H)$  count feasible choices, including the empty choice, on each additional endpoint component. Component factorization gives the exact global count
$$\#\{\text{nonempty global bundles}\}
=
(k+1)(l+1)\prod_{H\ne C}N(H)-1.
\tag{23}$$
Additional feasible exterior promotions can also be appended to  $U$ , producing distinct global bundles with the same square-removing restriction to  $C$ .Your text introduces restrictions to  $C$  before making the uniqueness claims, so the intended local reading is supported. I would nevertheless carry that qualifier into the final count and uniqueness sentences.5. Composition, factorization, and occupied-contact ownership check outCompatible unionFor individually feasible bundles  $B_i$ , with deleted mate sets  $D_i$ ,
$$A_{\mathrm{union}}
=
A\setminus\bigcup_iD_i
\subseteq A\setminus D_i.$$
Disjoint matching-edge sets prevent a promoted vertex from being deleted by another bundle. Every promoted vertex therefore sees no more occupied neighbors in the union than in its individually feasible bundle. Original  $T$ -vertices also only lose occupied neighbors.This proves feasibility and the additive count.The extension to shared edges with identical orientations is correct after deduplication. In that extension, the increase is the number of distinct selected matching edges; the sum of the original bundle sizes applies only in the disjoint-edge statement, as your note already specifies.Component factorizationThe necessity direction is correct and important. If a promoted endpoint lies in  $H$ , every original endpoint adjacent to it lies in  $H$ . Original  $T$  persists, and original blanks stay blank. Therefore deleting endpoints in another component cannot change its occupied neighborhood.The compatible-union lemma supplies sufficiency.The only convention to add is that an empty restriction is treated as the feasible identity move. A nonempty global bundle can of course have empty restrictions on some components.Occupied-contact ownershipThe proof is correct in both cases:An endpoint contact belongs to the component of every endpoint to which it is adjacent.A  $T$ -contact can touch at most one endpoint, since endpoints are occupied and its occupied degree is at most one.Using the supplied canonical guard criterion, failure of both colors supplies an occupied guard of each color for every selected strip. Opposite colors distinguish the two choices within one component; ownership distinguishes choices belonging to different components. Hence the  $2L$  bound and the separate  $L$ -per-color bounds follow.This proves distinctness of occupied vertices. It supplies no injective assignment to aligned tiles and no charge budget. Your separation of those conclusions is correct.6. The frozen-contact example is geometrically correctThe support incidences are exactly:Matching endpointIts two selected supports $(-2,0)$  $(-3,0),\,(-2,-1)$  $(-1,0)$  $(-1,1),\,(0,0)$  $(2,1)$  $(1,1),\,(2,2)$  $(3,1)$  $(3,0),\,(4,1)$ The eight selected vertices are pairwise nonadjacent, and each has exactly its indicated endpoint neighbor. Each endpoint has two permanent  $T$ -supports, so every endpoint is universally frozen immediately.The two matching edges form distinct endpoint components. Their exclusive contacts  $(0,0)$  and  $(1,1)$  occupy opposite corners of the same aligned tile, whose other two vertices are blank.Translation by  $(4,2)$  places all occupied sites in rows  $1,\ldots,8$  and columns  $1,\ldots,4$ , fitting inside a  $10\times6$  rectangle with blank padding. $$|T|=8,\qquad |M|=2,\qquad |T|+|M|=10$$
are correct.The only uncheckable numerical label from this excerpt alone is “charge zero”: the charge function is not included. If the existing ledger assigns zero to that occupancy, the claimed zero-charge obstruction follows directly.Recommended clarificationsThese are statement and exposition refinements, not repairs to the freezing or classification proof:State that empty component restrictions are feasible identity moves.Add the forced-blank-contact argument when extending the family to arbitrary feasible exteriors.Keep “supported on  $C$ ” explicit in the count, maximum-increase, and uniqueness statements under that extension.Make the reflected right-half argument precise for  $k\ne l$ , for example using (18).Cite or display the charge convention used for the  $2T,0P$  tile.No substantive mathematical revision is needed for the universal freezing certificate, the implication equivalence, or the exact  $(k+1)(l+1)-1$  classification.
